Hype
HIPE
noun / adjective (Gen X slang)
Origin uncertain: often traced to hyperbole (Greek, "a throwing beyond"), and also to 1920s American underworld slang, where hype meant a swindle and hyped up (from hypo, a hypodermic needle) meant stimulated. By the 1960s hype meant extravagant promotion. Hip-hop made it double-edged in the late 1980s: Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back) warned against media spin, while the same scene used hype as an adjective for exciting, energetic ("the crowd was hype").

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hype has two faces in Gen X speech. As a noun it means inflated promotion — the hype around a movie, a sneaker, a prizefight. As an adjective it means exciting, charged up: "That show was hype." Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) captured the first sense for a generation: the headlines, the ads, and the image-makers will mislead you. The Christian observation is that this is sound biblical counsel. "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1Th 5:21). "Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God" (1Jn 4:1). Proverbs describes the man who hypes himself: "Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain" (Pro 25:14) — big thunderheads over a dry field. John names the engine underneath all of it: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1Jn 2:16), which advertising has always known how to stir. And Jeremiah names the only thing worth boasting about: "let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:24). There is one Name that never disappoints its billing; the gospel is the only announcement in history that turned out bigger than the advance notice. A father can say to his son: don’t believe the hype — not the world’s, and not your own; but believe the Word, and boast in the Lord.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X / hip-hop slang for inflated promotion (n.) or exciting, charged up (adj.), possibly from hyperbole; Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) echoes Scripture’s prove all things (1Th 5:21).

HYPE, n. and adj. (Gen X slang, 1980s–1990s; hip-hop) As n., exaggerated promotion, buzz; as adj., exciting, energetic, charged up. "Don’t believe the hype." "The crowd was hype."

Hyped / hyped up, excited; to hype, to promote extravagantly. Possibly from hyperbole; compare 1920s hype (swindle) and hypo (hypodermic).

Public Enemy, "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988): the slogan of media skepticism for a generation.

Webster 1828: HYPERBOLE, n. hyper’boly. [Gr. excess, to throw beyond, to exceed.] In rhetoric, a figure of speech which expresses much more or less than the truth, or which represents things much greater or less, better or worse than they really are. …

Decode for parents: teach your children to test the hype — the world’s and their own — and to boast only in the Lord.

Key Scripture

1Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

1Jn 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Pro 25:14 — "Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift is like clouds and wind without rain."

1Jn 2:16 — "For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world."

Jer 9:24 — "But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Hype is the art of making things look bigger than they are; Scripture tests every claim, exposes the boaster as clouds without rain, and reserves glorying for knowing the LORD.

expand to see more

Clouds without rain. Hype is the economy of the promise that does not deliver: the movie that was not as good as the trailer, the product that was not as life-changing as the ad, the celebrity whose image outran his character. Proverbs saw it three thousand years ago (Pro 25:14). Public Enemy’s warning was right as far as it went; the Christian adds that the human heart is also a hype machine, and we oversell ourselves most of all.

Glory rightly placed. Jeremiah forbids the three great self-promotions — wisdom, might, riches (Jer 9:23) — and permits one boast: that a man knows the LORD (Jer 9:24). Here is the only thing that cannot be overhyped. The gospel did not overpromise; the empty tomb outran every expectation. Teach children to discount the world’s hype, distrust their own, and spend their excitement on what will bear its weight.

Greek hyperbole (a throwing beyond) and 1920s hype / hypo → 1960s promotional hype → Public Enemy’s "Don’t Believe the Hype" (1988) and the adjective hype; Scripture: prove all things (1Th 5:21).
